claims.text: High-entropy alloys contain at least five principal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios.
The proposed precursor contains more than five noble-metal salts or complexes.
Rapid heating followed by fast cooling suppresses atomic mobility during cooling.
Suppressed atomic mobility forces simultaneous decomposition or reduction of the metal precursors.
Rapid cooling kinetically traps a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
A slower cooling rate increases atomic diffusion.
Increased diffusion during slower cooling permits relaxation toward equilibrium.
Relaxation during slower cooling causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Slower cooling can produce crystal structures different from the fast-cooled structure.
High temperature promotes rapid precursor decomposition or reduction and atomic intermixing of the noble metals.
Atomic mobility during cooling controls the nucleation and growth of elemental aggregates versus kinetic trapping of a solid solution.
The fast-cooled baseline will have a homogeneous elemental distribution and a single phase, potentially FCC.
The slower-cooled sample will show more phase separation, elemental clustering, or secondary crystal structures than the fast-cooled baseline.
Fast cooling rates on the order of 10^4–10^5 K/s are an appropriate baseline for the proposed comparison.
Temperatures above approximately 1100 K and millisecond-range heating are appropriate for precursor fusion in this regime.
Differences among precursor redox potentials and thermal decomposition temperatures can impede simultaneous decomposition or reduction.
The mechanism may not apply under near-equilibrium slow-heating and slow-cooling conditions.
A sufficiently short heating duration prevents diffusion before cooling.

contradictions.description: The material and boundary fields require more than five elements, whereas the conditions field permits at least five elements, including exactly five.

The mechanism says high-temperature processing ensures atomic intermixing, which requires atomic transport, while the boundary states that heating is sufficiently short to prevent pre-cooling diffusion without distinguishing beneficial intermixing from segregation.
